name: Arete Foundation for Arts and Culture
funding: Small non-profit founded 2012 by Reem Gibriel, Khaled Mattawa and Nedal Swehli; AFAC grants in 2012, 2016 and 2019 (NACP National Fund).
watch: Fills the Libya gap; still active in Tripoli, with a 2 Mar 2023 symposium at Dar Al Funoon. Replaces Townhouse, Cairo, which has no record after 2018.
records_note: No Arete website was located; the only records are AFAC's grantee page and an events listing, with no reports, accounts, funders or board.

name: Hayy Jameel
funding: Arts complex opened 6 Dec 2021, built and run by Art Jameel and paid for by the Jameel family (Abdul Latif Jameel, a car distribution and diversified group)
watch: Private family-funded arts complex with Saudi Arabia's first independent cinema. Separate site from Jameel Arts Centre in Dubai.
records_note: Hayy Jameel and its parent Art Jameel publish no annual reports, accounts or funder list; the site lists staff and the founder but no board.

name: Tashkeel
funding: Founded 2008, paid for privately by founder Sheikha Lateefa bint Maktoum plus project partners such as Van Cleef & Arpels (luxury) and Dubai Culture
watch: Non-profit studio, residency and gallery that also runs a commercial consultancy. ENOC, Dubai's state oil company, commissioned work through it for Expo 2020.
records_note: No annual reports, accounts, funder list or board; the about page names founder Sheikha Lateefa bint Maktoum and the team page lists staff only.

name: 421 Arts Campus (formerly Warehouse421)
funding: Opened 2015 in Mina Zayed as part of the Salama bint Hamdan Al Nahyan Foundation, a royal private foundation, with education and university programme partners
watch: Space for emerging artists, outside the big state museums. The backing foundation belongs to the UAE president's wife, Salama bint Hamdan.
records_note: It posts a 2021 to 2022 review and a 2023 study but no accounts; its partners page names sponsors from older projects without a date.

name: Al Riwaq Art Space
watch: Bahrain's longest-running independent contemporary art space, now a non-profit hub with studios, a library and a cafe.
records_note: Al Riwaq publishes no annual reports, accounts, sponsor list or board; its partnerships page names only an events collaborator.

name: Contemporary Art Platform (CAP)
funding: Private non-profit founded 2011 by Amer Al-Huneidi; shows co-hosted with the Lebanese Business Council, Tanmia charity and UNHCR (2024)
watch: One of Kuwait's largest independent exhibition spaces, in the Shuwaikh Industrial design district, with a public art-book library.
records_note: CAP Kuwait publishes no annual reports, accounts, funder list or board; its about page calls it a non-profit private organization.

name: Katuaq Greenland Cultural Centre
funding: About 33.6k cinema visits in 2023. Funded by Greenland's Self-Government and Kommuneqarfik Sermersooq (2M DKK each extra in 2026), plus GrønlandsBANKEN and Air Greenland.
watch: A self-owning foundation; its board is appointed by the Self-Government, the municipality, Visit Greenland and EPI. Bank (not under campaign) and state airline as sponsors.
records_note: Annual management reports 2018 to 2023 give results without full accounts; two unlabelled undated sponsor logos; the board is named in the 2023 report.

name: Tjibaou Cultural Centre (ADCK)
funding: Operating budget about 400M XPF (~US$3.6M) in 2026. Run by the public agency ADCK; the French State pays 68% of a 405M XPF renovation (2025).
watch: Renzo Piano building from 1998, run by the Kanak culture agency ADCK. It is being renovated through 2027 and stays open during the works.
records_note: The centre's site carries no annual reports, accounts, funder list or board; the 2026 budget and State renovation share come only from press coverage.

name: Musée de Tahiti et des Îles – Te Fare Iamanaha
funding: A public museum of French Polynesia. Its renovation, reopened in 2023, cost 844M XPF under the State–Country project contract (2020), with a friends' association.
watch: Reopened in 2023 with loans from the British Museum, Cambridge MAA and the Quai Branly, including the A'a statue from Rurutu.
records_note: No annual reports or funder list; the government's public-bodies report carries a one-page 2024 financial summary; no board is named.

name: Papua New Guinea National Museum and Art Gallery
funding: A state statutory body funded by the PNG government. Australia paid for its 2015–2018 refurbishment, which reopened on 12 Oct 2018.
watch: Australia paid for the building in the 1970s and for its pre-APEC refit in 2018.
records_note: Its site is down; archived copies show no reports, accounts or funder list, and a Board of Trustees page that names no one.

name: Fiji Museum
funding: A statutory body on a government grant (F$697,525 operating plus F$500,000 capital in 2018/19). Its digitisation has run on a US Ambassadors Fund grant since 2021.
watch: Its US-funded digitisation grant runs out in Sept 2026, and the museum is seeking F$300k to continue to 2028. UNESCO is also a partner.
records_note: No reports, accounts or funders on its site; annual reports for 2015 to 2017 went to Parliament, later ones lapsed; no trustees named.

name: Oceania Centre for Arts, Culture and Pacific Studies (USP)
funding: A small unit of the University of the South Pacific (established 1997). Its 2026 residency is co-funded with Creative New Zealand and Creative Australia.
watch: Hosts the 2026 Oceania Pacific Arts Residency. USP's own pages blocked automated reads.
records_note: The centre has no records of its own; parent USP posts annual reports, audited statements for 2005 to 2025 and names its Council.
